en: In the Māṇḍūkī Śikṣā belonging to the Atharvaveda, three tempos are enumerated: fast, medium, and slow;
among these, the first, the fast tempo, is praised according to the traditional sequence.
The medium tempo consists of a single interval, while the slow tempo has two intervals;
a wise person should not employ this [slow tempo] if they desire excellence of phonemes.
The fast tempo is for the purpose of practice, while the slow tempo is for comprehension.
The middle [pace], however, is for the purpose of practice; its utterance is not otherwise. The Aindra style is the middle pace, while the Prājāpatya is slow;
the Agnimāruta style is censured in all treatises.
However, in the slow tempo, the faults are not revealed, whereas in the fast tempo, the phonemes are not easily perceived.
Therefore, having abandoned both the fast and the slow tempos, a person should employ the medium tempo.
Indeed, all tempos are declared to be free from fault.
Especially by the wise chanters of the Sāmans, Khadyota, Suvaktra, and Śikṣaka, the seven musical notes are sung according to the Sāman verses;
however, only four meters are used there, three being excluded.
The six notes— Ṣaḍja, Ṛṣabha, Gāndhāra, Madhyama, Pañcama, Dhaivata, and Niṣāda— are the seven notes here in the Sāmans.
The peacock cries out in Ṣaḍja, and cows low in Ṛṣabha.
The goat bleats in Gāndhāra, while the cry of the crane is in Madhyama (9).
At the time when the flowers are in full bloom, the cuckoo calls in the fifth note (Pañcama);
the horse brays in Dhaivata, and the elephant trumpets in Niṣāda (10).
From the nose comes Gāndhāra, and likewise Madhyama from the chest;
the fifth note is said to arise from the chest, the head, and the throat;
Dhaivata arises from the forehead and so forth, while Niṣāda possesses its own specific form.
The Ṣaḍja note has the luster of a lotus petal, the Ṛṣabha is tawny like a parrot,
the Gāndhāra is golden-hued, and the Madhyama has the brilliance of a kunda flower.
The Pañcama should be black, while the Dhaivata is yellow in color.

The *niṣāda* has the luster of all colors; these are the [notes] according to their respective colors. (14) Now, the *kruṣṭa* (*ṣaḍja*) is on the thumb of Brahmā; the *madhyama* note is on the thumb; the *gāndhāra* is on the forefinger; and the *pañcama* is on the middle finger. (15)
The *ṣaḍja* is on the ring finger (*anāmikā*), while the *dhaivata* is on the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*);
they know that which is the last one below it to be the *niṣāda*.
Thus, the first and the last vowels exist within the Vedic meters (*chandas*).
Those of the middle [register] cease according to the opinion of Paṇḍūka (17).
They say the second is *svarita*, the sixth is called *pracita*;
one should know *niṣāda* as high (*ucca*) and *ṣaḍja* is declared to be low (*nīca*) (18).

The accent is observed by those expert in the analysis of accents to be fourfold: acute (udātta), grave (anudātta), circumflex (svarita), and protracted (pracita). Having understood the accent according to its proper place, the movement of the hand is prescribed.
Having withdrawn the hand that was placed on the palm, one should fix the gaze upon it. (20) One should let the arm fall from one's own shoulder toward the sky with the gaze slightly lowered;
then, having extended all the fingers, one should move the circle of the hand. (21)
One should not touch the thumb with the fingers, for that is known to cause defects;
the wise man should place the thumb extended upward and slightly bent.
It is taught that the head [of the hand] should not be downward, nor should the fingers be spread apart.

One should form the hand with its palm facing upward, slightly raised, with the fingers clearly visible and colored, bearing its own natural marks, and extending toward the region of the span (prādeśa);
that which is above another [finger] should be placed to the north or east of the thumb. 23–24.
One should move the hand only a span’s distance, reaching no further than that measure; otherwise,
there may be the faults of the hands known as *culuna*, *sphuṭī*, *daṇḍī*, *svastikā*, and the form of a *muṣṭikā* (fist), while the seventh is the fault of cutting with an axe.
Withdrawing his limbs like a tortoise, he should firmly restrain his movements, his gaze, and his mind;
he should not shake his head or feet, and he should avoid defects of the mouth.
The wise man should move his hand along the front of his nose.
One should utter the subtle phonemes toward the right ear,
making the hearing follow the speech and making the mind follow the speech;
then, making the gaze follow the hands, one should utter [the syllables] like a footstep.
As are the hands, so is the voice; one must avoid making it empty.
Wherever the hands are situated, there the voice is held; both the tone and the hand occur simultaneously. 29–30.
One who has fallen from the correct placement of the hand (mudrā) or fallen from the correct accents does not enjoy the fruit of the Veda;
he who studies while devoid of the proper hand-gestures and bereft of vowels and consonants is consumed by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas and enters a low womb.

If one should recite the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāman, and other Vedas without using one's hands, that Brāhmaṇa remains untruthful as long as he does not find his own voice. When the Veda is being studied with the hand, one should employ the correct accents and phonemes.
Purified by the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, he goes to the world of Brahman;
from tone to tone he proceeds with a smooth transition of vowels, without harshness. He should make it continuous and even, like a subtle shadow. 34.
One who knows the syllables, knows the pauses, and likewise the beginnings [of words], as well as the divisions of vowels and prosodic measures—that Brahmin is worthy to speak.
[He should use twigs] of the mango, palāśa, bilva, apāmārga, and śirīṣa. (36–37)

Having risen in the morning and restrained his speech, one should use for cleaning the teeth [twigs from] the Khadira, Karañja, Kadamba, milky trees (kṣīrin), Arka, Karavīra, and especially the Kuṭaja. 38.
By that means, his articulation becomes subtle and sweet;
and no one would perceive any defect in him while he speaks, for his voice is neither too loud nor too low, being free from the flaw of uneven resonance.
One should employ a voice that is neither too sharp nor too soft; one should always speak in the morning with a tone residing in the chest, resembling the roar of a tiger;
and at midday, with a tone situated in the throat, similar to the cry of a cuckoo. 41.

One should know that the third libation is the *tāra*; it should always be employed with the crest-lock (*śikhaṇḍin*), using a sound equal to the soft tones of peacocks, swans, and the like, which is pleasant for the head.
Just as a tiger might carry off its cubs without piercing them with its fangs.
One should employ the phonemes in that same way, fearing both their dropping and their breaking [of articulation].
Thus the phonemes are to be employed: neither released nor oppressed.
By the correct employment of the phonemes, one is glorified in the world of Brahman.
On winding paths, one should not travel more than a *yojana* at a slow pace;
for a voice placed behind the back is not fit to utter the *prayoga*.
One should form the shape of a fist at the end of "mā," and dissolve it at the end of "takāra."

One should employ the letter *na* at the end on the right side of the nail; however, at the ends of *ka* and *ṣṭa*, one should perform the contraction of the fingertips. Likewise, it should be so for the ends of *ṅa*, *ṇa*, and *na*; but at the end of *mā*, there should be the pressing of the fingers. 46–47.

The wise practitioner should release each measure equally for both the upward expulsion and the downward expulsion; likewise, when both are accumulated, he should do so in that same manner. Furthermore, during the performance of short vowels and the anusvāra, there should be the contraction of the fingers.
The wise, however, have declared that there is a protraction of the forefinger (deśinī) over a long duration.
One who knows the application of the *saṃhitā* should not create a pause between words;
one should not understand it as "māṃsam" [meat], but rather point out "māṃse māṃsam" [flesh upon flesh]. 49–50.
Just as a boat moves evenly in the midst of currents when joined with a stream of oil, so should one employ the phonemes;
likewise, one should not produce a high-pitched vowel (*udātta*) from a high-pitched vowel, nor a circumflex (*svarita*) from a high-pitched vowel.

There is nothing lower than the low, nor is there anything higher than the high. (52) There is nothing higher than the high; how could there be anything lower than the low? There is no tone more modulated than the modulated, and no tremolo more trembling than the trembling. (53)

That which is udātta remains udātta; that which is svarita becomes low (nīca) within the word; that which is already nīca remains nīca; and that which is situated in a pracaya [group] is also nīca. 54.
Anudātta is anudātta, characterized by a lack of resonance and the non-striking of the udātta tones.

That which is unaccented (anudātta), unsupported, and devoid of the hair-like [nasal] quality of the sibilants and *s* and *ṣ*—this is the sixfold *svarita* arising precisely from the *anudātta*, for the *anudātta* itself is fourfold and twofold; this is what is enjoined by the Śāstra. (55–56)
One should know that what originates from a *svarita* is either a *pracita* *svarita*, or an *udātta*, or an *anudātta*; and know that which is *pracita* to be the Truth.
Those *anudātta* syllables which follow a *svarita* are like *udātta*.

All [the preceding vowels] undergo coalescence (*pracaya*), for no *udātta* accent is found [therein]. (58) When an *udātta* follows a *svarita* that is determined [as such], it is called *vikrama*; when an *udātta* follows a *svarita* that is determined [as such], that foot is indeed *vikrama*. (59)

One should indeed maintain the *vṛtta* (the syllable), perform the *upasparśa* (touching the nose), and utter the *udātta* accent; one should maintain it in a single syllable and not utter what has already been maintained even in the case of a vowel.
From the very beginning, one should perform the *nyāsa* (placement) even when there are many fixed [syllables].

The remainder is stated to be as in the first case, both in those words and in even [words]. A high tone is called *udātta*, a low tone is called *anudātta*, and where the vowel remains, that is called *svarita*. The consonants follow wherever that vowel resides.
The high tone (udātta), the low tone (anudātta), and indeed the circumflex tone (svarita)—
those who contemplate syllables say that this threefold tonality (traisvarya) is the primary element.
However, when there arises a single state at the junction of two tones, [it is called a single tone].
Even an acute vowel falls under the power of a grave vowel in euphonic combinations (sandhi);
just as a powerful king seizes the kingdom of one who is weak,
so too a vowel, having encountered a consonant, takes it away— of this there is no doubt.
In the application of the Ākhyānas, one should extract the vowel according to the preceding accent, limited to sixteen syllables; however, where there is a conjunction [of consonants],
one should extract the vowel that precedes the low (nīca) tone, as well as the low pause (nīcāvagraha).
One should know that which is to be slain as being free from high and low notes (uccā-vagraha).
One should not strike it, nor should one strike it away; one should not sing over it, nor should one cause it to tremble.
These two are to be accomplished simultaneously; this is what is enjoined by the scripture.
There are eight places of articulation for the phonemes: the chest, the throat, the head, as well as the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate.
Furthermore, in the production of phonemes, there are four types of articulatory organs (karaṇa).
Closed (*saṃvṛta*) and open (*vivṛta*), touched (*spṛṣṭa*) and untouched (*aspṛṣṭa*):
the production of the [first four] consonants is "touched," while that of the semivowels (*antasthā*) is otherwise.
Regarding the *yama*s, they say it is "svarita" (intermediate), and for the sibilants (*viroṣman*), it is "open."
I shall proclaim the seven musical notes (svaras) and their relative strengths and weaknesses, as well as the characteristics of all of them; listen to me as I describe them correctly.
They are: the *abhinihita*, the *prāśliṣṭa*, the *jātya*, the *kṣaipra*, and the *pādavṛtta*.

The sixth is *tairovyañjana* and the seventh is *tirovirāma*. (72) Where they elide the vowel *a* after *e* and *o* when followed by a following acute-accented vowel (*abhyāsa-samudātta*), and where that *a* is accompanied by a *repha* (the sound *r*), they know that [elision] as *abhinihita*. (74)
Wherever one should see the vowel *i* joined with *i* itself—

even if it is an acute (*udātta*) following an unaccented (*anudātta*) or even when it is closely joined (*prāśliṣṭa*)— it becomes a circumflex (*svarita*), provided that the syllable is accompanied by the letter *y* or the sound *dhaṃ*.

Nor is there an acute accent before it in the case of a *jāti* vowel; however, when the vowels *i* and *u* (along with their long forms) become *y* and *v* respectively before an unaccented suffix, know that this is always the characteristic of the *kṣaipra* svarita. 76–77.

One should know that as *pādavṛtta* where there is a svarita [vowel] following a svarita, or where there is a hiatus (*vivṛti*) but [the next word] is in *saṃhitā*; they, however, place the pause (*avagraha*) in this [latter case]. That which occurs in the second syllable, consisting of one and a half [mātrās], preceded by an udātta— 78.
The phrase "tairovyañjana" is the essence; it is like the sequence "dadhi-madhu.
Where there is a circumflex accent (*svarita*) immediately following an *avagraha*, one should recognize that as a *tirovirāma*; Prajāpati is the authority for this.
When there is a low-pitched vowel between two high-pitched vowels where there is an avagraha, it should be treated as a *kampa*; the example is "tanūnām".
Likewise, a palatal vowel should be treated as such, though the *kampa* is not designated by its own specific name.
That [sound] produced by the palate is the kampita; "ejata" is the illustration.
Then there is the sarva-tīkṣṇa, followed by the abhinihita; thereafter the prāśliṣṭa is mentioned.
Then both the jātya and the kṣaipra are indeed softer. 82–83.

Then, the *vyañjana* (consonant) following a *svāra* (vowel) that is more *mṛdu* (soft) is called *pādavṛta-mṛdu-tara*; this is the relative strength and weakness of the *svāra*. Furthermore, the placement known as *kaṇṭhe-nikṣepa* (throat-deposition) must be performed.
After the placement [of the vowel], one should strike [the consonant] on the ground, just like the mark of a stake (śaṅkupada).
Of those [vowels]— the *prāśliṣṭa*, the *jātya*, the *kṣaipra*, the *praśliṣṭa*, and the *abhinihita*—
one should determine a single portion for each when they are followed by an acute-accented vowel (*udātta-upasthita*).

That "ya" which follows a word ending in a consonant (halanta), as well as that which occurs at the beginning of a word or in avagrahas, is known as *yonya* when it is different from the preceding "ya" itself. This applies to the beginning of a verse-quarter (*pāda*), the beginning of a word, and within conjunct consonants (*saṃyoga*) or avagrahas. (87)

That which is to be known as *yaḥ-śabda* is remembered as *yonyaḥ-sa-yaḥ*. Furthermore, where there is a *saṃhitā* at the end of a word containing the sound *savit-* or *prātar-*, and the words therein end with the letter *r*, that word is called *riphita*. 88–89.
If any internal sound (antaḥśabda) should be accented on the first syllable,
they do not desire the letter *r* there, either in *saṃhitā* or in individual words (90).
For the *anusvāra* is indeed a fault [in such cases], except when it occurs after the letter *h* and others.
"Aṃhomucaḥ," "vātaraṃhāḥ," and "daṃhaśceti" are the illustrations [of the long vowel].
An anusvāra should also be applied; there are three types: short, long, and protracted (pluta). For example: "ayaṃ rājā yaśormāsaṃ kṣatriyāṇāṃ dhanūṃṣi ca. 91–92.
Furthermore, four types of reversals (vivṛtti) should be known in their proper sequence;
I shall describe their characteristics individually according to their names: Pipīlikā, Pākavatī, and likewise Vatsānusāriṇī. (93)
Indeed, there are four types of *vivṛtti* (turning):
*anusṛtavatsā*, *vatsānusṛtā*, *hrasvā*, and *jaghane vatsānusāriṇī*; furthermore, there is *pākavatī* at the front, *pipīlikamadhyā* in the middle, and *ubhayadīrghā* at both ends. 94–95.
Where a long vowel is seen at the beginning and the end of the forenoon [meter], it should be known as *vatsānusṛtā*; when reversed, it is called *anusāriṇī*.
One should designate that which has short vowels at both ends as *yavamadhyā*. 96.
By those same two long [lines], that *pipīlikā* (ant-line) is to be known;
it is seen like lightning in the midst of weapons, like a gem on a thread.
This is the division (*cheda*) of the *vivṛttis*, just as a pair of scissors is among children. 96–97.

The letter *m* becomes an *anusvāra* when followed by *yakāra*, *ūṣman*, or *visarga* as suffixes; it does not become an *anusvāra* before the letter *l*, nor does there occur the substitution of the nasal of the same class (*parasavarṇa*) before the semivowels (*sparśa*) or the sibilants (*uttama*).
(98) Wherever the two *ūṣman* letters *dh* and *y* are seen following a vowel, they are [treated] as having vowels as their initial elements (*udaya*).

The two phonemes *ṛ* and *ḷ* should likewise be understood as established as *svarabhakti*. One should recognize that [the *svarabhakti*] is short if its duration is one *mātrā*; one should understand it correctly and avoid the two faults. (99–100)
When one perceives this correctly, there is the illustration "śatavalīśa";
likewise, the letter *a* and the letter *u* are [to be seen] as separated and open. Furthermore, there are the *kariṇī*, the *kurviṇī*, and the *hāriṇī* of the letters *la* and *ha*.
One should know the *hariṇī* from the letters *ṛ*, *ṣa*, *ya*, *dya*, *ha*, *ri*, *ta*, *la*, *śa*, and *ka*. That which consists of the letters *ra* and *sa* is called *haṃsapadā*.
One should designate that which consists of the letters *ra* and *śa* as *kākinī*.

When the *ṛ*-vowel occurs as a suffix (*pratyaya*), the *repha* (the sound *r*) is conjoined with *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*; in that case, the sequence should be understood as the former [order] and not the latter, as taught by the wise.
(104) In the conjunction of *repha* and the sibilants (*ūṣman*), there is the *svarabhakti* (vowel-fragment) and indeed a non-sequential [conjunction].
Therein, the demonstration of examples is as follows: "Varṣo" and "barhiḥ" (105).

One should know the letter *ra* (*repha*) in the arising of vowels (*svarodaya*), and the letter *ṛ* (*ṛkāra*) in the arising of consonants (*vyañjanodaya*); one should specifically designate the letter *ra* (*repha*) between vowels and consonants (106).
Emission (*obhāva*), opening (*vivṛti*), *ś*, *ṣ*, *s*, *r*, *v*, *j* (the root of the tongue), and the labio-dental (*upadhmāna*)— these are the eightfold movement of the *ūṣman* sounds.
Furthermore, there is the substitution of *ṣ*, the substitution of *ṇ*, euphonic combination (*upācāra*), and likewise the lengthening of vowels.

That pada upon which they settle is the defining characteristic of a compound (samāsa). One should know that a pada ending in a vowel, if it follows the letter *u* or others and involves a connection between two [words], is such [a compound];
any other [pada] is clearly characterized by a sibilant (*ūṣman*). 108–109.
Like a compacted mass of wood, the phonemes—which are subject to the power of conjunction—should be emitted as if they were a single phoneme when joined in pairs;
this occurs when the twenty consonants ending in *k* are followed by a vowel situated in the subsequent position within a word. (110)
One should recognize the red color; one must not swallow the preceding syllable.
(111) When one perceives the red color situated together with a reversal, one should recognize it as the end of a consonant, as in the example "gomām̐. (112)
Just as a woman from Saurāṣṭra pronounces "arām," so should the musical notes (raṅgas) be employed, excluding the syllable 'aṅka'.
From the nose arises the note raṅga, which has a sound equal to that of a bronze gong (kaṃsa).

A soft [vowel] should have two mātrās; "vṛṣṭimām" is the illustration. One should know that which precedes a conjunct consonant to be short and light; one should know that which follows such a conjunct to be heavy; here they apply this rule invariably.

A single *mātrā* is to be known as light; it becomes heavy when followed by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*), or when followed by another vowel, or when ending in a consonant. A long vowel (*dīrgha*) consists of two *mātrās*, while a protracted vowel (*pluta*) consists of three. Furthermore, if there is a conjunction of a stop (*sparśa*) with a following stop in due order, [the preceding syllable is considered heavy].
One should know that there are likewise four Yamas there in successive order:
one should know the first as Rukva, the others know the second as Nṛcakṣas, they call the third Padma, and the last Śaṅkhaghna. (117–118)
Where the final letters of the consonant groups (varga-anta) are seen joined with śa, ṣa, and sa,
there the *yamās* turn back, like kinsmen from a cremation ground.
[The letter] following a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is its own [independent] meaning, and it is the leader of the conjunction.
However, for a consonant that is joined [with another], a preceding vowel is not desired.
Whether it be a vowelization (*svaraṇa*) or a falling away (*patana*), this occurs only in the case of rising [consonants] or when they are equal;
it is observed within a single word and never occurs with a preceding syllable. 120–121.
There are twenty-one consonants (varṇas) for which doubling is prescribed: the first, middle, and last letters of each group, as well as *ya*, *la*, *va*, and *śa*, *ṣa*, and *sa*.
However, doubling is never observed to occur for the letter *ra* or for the letter *ha*.

One should never conjoin the second letters of a class with the fourth, nor the fourth with the third, nor the second with the first; furthermore, one should not conjoin the first, the last, or the third letter with its own corresponding vowel. 124–125.
In *dṛpsau*, *apsarāyām*, *aśabde*, *viśvapsyan*, and *atra virapaśine*,
Kāśyapa maintains that there is no elision (*abhinighāta*) because it is prohibited;
likewise, where consonants (*sparśa*) are joined on both sides with *śa*, *ṣa*, or *sa* sounds.
In that regard, the first sequence should be known, and not another, as taught by the wise.
Immediately following [the vowel], there should be a svarita [accent] joined with the letter *ṛ* and the consonant *r*.
That which is preceded by the conjunction of the vowel *ṛ* and the consonant *r* should arise with a consonant.

One should know that in the syllable *ṛ* it is light, while in the syllable *r* it is designated as heavy. When *ṛ* and *r* are joined, and a consonant arises before them, one should know that in the syllable *śṛ* it is light, while in the syllable *r* it is designated as heavy. 129. Śṛkāre laghu tadvidyād rephe tadgurusañjñakam.

It does not apply when there is a vowel (*svara*), nor between two letters of the same class (*varga-savarṇa*), nor at a pause (*virāma*). Nor does it apply before the letter *r*, the *anusvāra*, or the *visarjanīya*—though some say it applies everywhere in these cases. One should not move the eyebrows, nor the ears, forehead, or nose; one should not tremble the lips, nor should one contract them.
One should not distort the face, nor behave like a naked ascetic; one should not step with the feet visible, nor speak with external words.
One should not be harsh in speech, nor speak in a loud voice; one should not stare with unblinking eyes, nor practice arrogance.
One should walk with the gait of an elephant, being strong, untiring, and free from anger, fatigue, grief, joy, and fear.
One should not utter a word with a harsh sound from the very beginning; one should not speak with the nose constantly engaged [in snoring];

nor, when afflicted by fatigue at the end of a word, should one pant or repeatedly gasp even after a syllable has been spoken. One should not over-compress the phonemes, nor should one pronounce them indistinctly.
The wise man should pronounce the phonemes evenly, smoothly, and without ambiguity.
He should present the first mantras as if they were not yet arisen, and he should recognize them in such a way that even a non-human being would perceive them with his mind. 134–135.
In the same way, they say that when a fifth [vowel] is observed in a traditional source (āgama), one should treat it as a second [vowel]; the example for this is the word "sītā.
A phoneme which is uttered in the mere twinkling of an eye—
That which consists of one measure (mātrā) is short; that which is twice as long is called protracted (pluta). In the avagraha, the duration is half a measure; between words, it is one measure.
Likewise, between two hemistichs or two quarters of a verse, it is one and a half measures; but at the end of a ṛc, it shall be three measures.
The blue jay speaks with one mora, the crow spoke with two moras, and the peacock is to be known as having three moras; such is this summary of moras.
In some cases it occurs by the division of a quarter-verse, in some cases by half a verse, and in some cases within a single word.

The pause (*virāma*) is traditionally taught as being fivefold: occurring after a certain meaning, after a certain word, and [the others]. These are employed in Vedic meter in their respective order and are designated as "delays" (*kṣepa*);
they should be applied with a pause so that the metrical flow (*vṛtti*) is not disrupted.

I shall declare further faults regarding *mañjñāna*; listen: the manifestation of the vowel (*svara*), as well as the *anusvāra* and *ya-mā* (the nasal *m*), [if performed] with a broken quality, a distracted quality, or too coldly, like a small drop of *soma*. 142.
One should pause at the sound *ī* [in the word] *pratiśuklā*; this is the fifth [rule]. 143.

In the case of doubt regarding the word *viśvānām*, it should be treated as a neuter half-verse; whether preceding or following, all instances of *viśvā* are without the *ṣ* sound (*nirūṣmakāḥ*). 144.
When a word ending in the letter *n* is followed by a vowel or by the suffixes *ś*,
*ṣ*, *s*, or *p*, a short *mātrā* (anusvāra) should be employed.
There are two *takāras* and two *thakāras*, and the fifth [consonant] is not a *yama*.
Those who contemplate syllables call this "entirety" (kṛtsna) a conjunction.
When the word *pūrva* ending in the letter *ka* is followed by the suffix *ṅa*, one should apply the augment *ṅa* to the *ṅa*; the example is *vāṅkma*. 146–147.

When a word ending in the letter *ṭ* precedes and the suffix *ṇa* follows, one should apply the augment *ṇ* to the [suffix]; for example, *vaṇ mahām̐*. When a word ending in the letter *t* precedes and the suffix *na* follows...
One should apply the augment *na* where there is the example *yat na*.
(149) When a word ending in *m* precedes and the suffix *ma* follows, one should apply the augment *m*, as in the example *tannaṣṭumpam*. (150)
Having seen the final *kaṭatapa* and likewise the supreme *ṅamaṇanama*, those who contemplate the imperishable speak of the union with the self as the fifth.
From the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), one becomes free from fear; from the sacred tradition, one becomes free from fear. 151.
One becomes fearless and sweet-toned; through sweetness, one attains success.
The transmission of the tradition is the best, as is the precise determination of the phonemes. One should practice this with vigilance; this is the instruction of the Teacher. 152–153.
He was perfected in the traditional scriptures and understood the essence of the sacred texts;
like milk in a conch shell, he possessed the essence of the Vedic meters.
His speech was produced with the subtle articulation of the dental-labial sounds, and it was sweet and youthful.
They say that the nature of a student is one thing, while that which is produced by the teacher is another. (155) They call a young student a "learner," but an old one a "thinker of syllables.
A logician is called one who has heard much from others; thus there are many kinds of beggars. (156)

One who is not hideous, nor has protruding lips, nor is nasalized throughout, nor stammers, nor has a bound tongue, is fit to utter the applications [of mantras]. One whose nature is auspicious and whose teeth and lips are beautiful [is likewise fit]. (157)
He by whom [the truth] has been studied according to reality will master the training.

Some are superior in their scriptural traditions (āgama), others are superior in their insights (vijñāna), and others are superior in the excellence of their practice; there is no cause for pride in thinking, "I am [the best]. 158–159.
The Veda that has come from a good source, is properly consumed, well-recited, and well-established,
when employed with a beautiful voice by a skilled speaker, truly shines forth.
(160) But that which has come from a bad source is burnt, and is devoured by those of foul complexion.
There is no liberation for him from sin, as if from a venomous snake.
Those who have received the knowledge of the Tīrthas but are constantly devoid of practice become invincible, like perfectly solid mountains. 161–162.

One who desires knowledge should not be one who delays over food, nor should he be bound by women; he should move like a swan in the sky. Just as noble horses sleep for only half a day and night, so should he be.
Sleep does not remain long in the eyes of those who seek excellence.
Fearing people as one fears a snake, fearing women as one fears hell, and fearing even sweet things as one fears poison—he shall master his learning. (164–165)
Knowledge that has been multiplied a thousandfold and refined a hundred times will come to the tip of one's tongue, like water flowing from high ground to a low place;
it becomes multiplied a hundredfold when practiced, but a thousandfold when retained.
He who studies even a thousand verses with a hundred repetitions remains established both in this world and after death (verse 167).
Furthermore, he who studies in a whisper and with haste, as if without weariness— even when dealing with thousands of forms that are subject to doubt— remains steadfast (verse 168).
And those whose power of comprehension is not exceedingly sharp,
who do not recite [the text] hundreds of times even after having acquired it,
and who do not abandon sleep as if it were a dear friend; [for them, this is difficult].
Such people reach old age in the houses of their teachers;
those men who are greedy and fierce do not acquire the fivefold knowledge, nor do those who are lazy, free from disease, yet possess a corrupted mind.
Recitation beyond a thousand [times], constant contemplation,
and recitation together with authoritative masters— this is remembered as the threefold *dhāraṇā*.
Just as one finds water in the earth by digging with a spade, [so too does one find the truth through these means].
In this way, one who desires to hear acquires the knowledge residing in the guru.
A tiny ant may travel a thousand yojanas slowly, yet even Vainateya, though flying, does not go a single step without walking.
By means of a single word, the wise man finds a hundred words;
by a thousand words, the fool does not find even one. Therefore, one should diligently study every word, every quarter-verse, and every half-verse. 174.
The unwise man attains wisdom, just as the ocean does by means of rivers.
(175) Perseverance is the root of prosperity; who could not dry up the ocean if they were to carry a metal-bound water-pot for days and nights? (176)

Through the power of practice, water causes the destruction even of mountains; what, then, cannot practice accomplish? Even that which is hard and rough becomes soft to the touch. (177) Teachers desire [the recitation] to be even, while scholars desire the division of words.
Women desire what is sweet; other people desire a loud proclamation.
(178) Knowledge is attained through six means: by attending upon a teacher, through yoga, by austerity, by serving the wise, by engaging in debate, and through desire. (179)
Through laziness, association with fools, fear, affliction by disease,
overeating, and pride— by these six, knowledge is destroyed.
(180) [Listen to] the instruction given by the frog, which illuminates the intellect of the wise.
"For he who knows the world of Brahmā in its true essence goes there.
Thus ends the Māṇḍūkī Śikṣā belonging to the Atharvaveda.
